Going steady
GOH-ing STED-ee
phrase (Silent Generation slang)
American courtship term. Steady for a regular sweetheart is recorded early in the twentieth century; the phrase going steady was the standard teenage term of the 1940s and 1950s for an exclusive dating relationship, often marked by a class ring worn on a chain or wrapped in yarn, or a letter jacket. In the postwar years it became the usual pattern of high-school romance, and it was understood as a step short of engagement.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1955, when a boy asked a girl to go steady, he gave her his class ring, and she wore it on a chain around her neck or wrapped the band in angora yarn so it would fit her finger. Everyone at school knew what it meant: they were a couple, and nobody else need ask her to the dance. Some of those couples married and are celebrating sixty years; many broke up by spring. Scripture has a great deal to say about this road, because it is the road to marriage. Marriage is a good goal: "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD" (Pro 18:22), and "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled" (Heb 13:4). The one to go steady with must share the faith: "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers" (2Co 6:14). And the long months of an exclusive teenage romance carry their own danger, which the Song warns of three times: "that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). Paul gives the standard for the whole season: "That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour" (1Th 4:4). Going steady at fourteen with no thought of marriage often stirred up love long before it could please. A grandparent can bless the ring on the chain and still counsel patience, purity, and prayer, pointing to Christ, the Bridegroom who keeps His promises.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American, 1940s–50s) for an exclusive teenage romance, marked by a class ring on a chain — a step on the road toward marriage, under the Song’s charge to stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please (Son 2:7).

expand to see more

GOING STEADY, v. phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s) Dating one person exclusively, often signified by wearing the other’s class ring or jacket; a stage short of engagement. "Jimmy gave me his class ring — we’re going steady!"

Decode for families: going steady was meant to lead somewhere; dating with no thought of marriage often led to heartbreak.

Key Scripture

Pro 18:22 — "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD."

Heb 13:4 — "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge."

2Co 6:14 — "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?"

Son 2:7 — "I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please."

1Th 4:4 — "That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;"

Modern Corruption

An honest courtship word, but the custom of long exclusive romances among young teenagers, far from marriage, often stirred up love before its time.

expand to see more

Going steady named something better than casual dating: loyalty to one person, publicly declared. Many lifelong marriages began with a class ring on a chain, and the word deserves a kind hearing.

The trouble lay in the age and the aim. Fourteen-year-olds going steady for a year with no prospect of marriage were pressed toward a closeness they were not ready to keep pure, and the breakups taught them to give their hearts away and take them back again. Scripture’s counsel is to wait for love’s proper time (Son 2:7), to choose a believer (2Co 6:14), and to walk the road to marriage in sanctification and honour (1Th 4:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English stede (place), stedig (firm) → English steady → early 20th c. steady, a regular sweetheart → 1940s–50s going steady, exclusive teenage dating.

1940s–50s: going steady; the class ring on a chain

Understood as a step short of pinned and engaged
